title: 'I Quit Indian Food and Got in the Best Shape of My Life': Delhi Man in Canada Sparks a Diet Debate
excerpt: Banshdeep Singh credits 18 months without Indian cooking — four high-protein meals a day in a calorie deficit — for his transformation. The internet is split on whether the cuisine or the convenience is the real story.
body:
• Banshdeep Singh, a Delhi native living in Canada, says he stopped cooking Indian food about 18 months ago — and credits the change with putting him in "the best shape of my life."
  • His routine: four meals a day, more than 150 grams of protein, and a sustained calorie deficit — which he says Indian home cooking made harder to control.
  • Singh's core argument is convenience, not cuisine: grocery shopping, prepping ingredients, spices and tadka "take a lot of time," and "it affects the body badly."
  • Nutritionists would push back on one point: no cuisine is inherently unfit — dal, paneer, chicken curries and roti can easily clear 150g of protein. The debate is about portion control and oil, not spices.

A Delhi man living in Canada has set off a furious debate about food, fitness and cultural identity after crediting his dramatic physical transformation to one decision: quitting Indian food.

The video

In a video shared on Instagram last month, Banshdeep Singh explained that he has not cooked Indian food in about a year and a half. "Maine last dedh saal se Indian khana banana aur chhoda hua hai," he said — I've stopped making Indian food for the last 18 months. "After that decision, I am in the best shape of my life," he wrote in the caption.

Singh described coming home after a long day with almost no energy left for exercise — until he saw his physique in the mirror. "When I look at myself in the mirror, and my body is looking so good, I feel like working harder," he said. His current routine: four meals a day, more than 150 grams of protein, and staying in a calorie deficit, fitted around his work and gym schedule.

His argument: it's about time and control

Singh's case against Indian cooking is practical rather than ideological. "Earlier, when I was cooking Indian food — first of all, it takes a lot of time," he said. "Secondly, you have to do so much grocery shopping for that. Then add spices and temper it. It affects the body badly." For someone trying to follow a tightly controlled diet, he argued, the process of assembling a full Indian meal — multiple ingredients, tadka, roti or rice — is a friction he can do without. His current meals, he said, leave him full and give him "mental satisfaction" he can't quite explain: "Pet bhi bhara hua hai aur mentally bhi satisfaction milti hai."

The backlash — and the fairer reading

The video divided the internet along a predictable fault line. Critics called it a rejection of his own food culture, pointing out that millions of people eat Indian food daily while staying fit — and that blaming "Indian khana" for weight gain confuses the cuisine with how much oil, sugar and refined carbs go into specific dishes. Supporters said Singh was being honest about his own constraints: a busy immigrant life, a strict protein target, and the genuine time cost of cooking traditional meals from scratch.

Nutritionists would likely side with the nuance. A home-cooked Indian diet — dal, chana, paneer, eggs, chicken curry, roti, sabzi — can comfortably exceed 150 grams of protein a day; the problem is rarely the cuisine and usually the portions, the ghee-to-dal ratio, and the extras. What Singh really eliminated, arguably, was not Indian food but imprecision.

The diaspora dimension

The debate resonates because it maps onto a real immigrant experience. Cooking the food of home abroad takes more time, more ingredients and more effort than it ever did in India — and for a generation of NRIs juggling long work hours, the siren call of meal-prep chicken and protein shakes is strong. Singh's video struck a nerve precisely because so many recognise the trade-off: comfort and identity on one side, convenience and control on the other.

The takeaway

Singh's transformation is real, and his candour about the effort behind it is useful. But the lesson isn't that Indian food is the enemy of fitness — it's that consistency beats cuisine. Whether the protein comes from a grilled chicken breast or a well-planned dal-and-paneer thali matters far less than whether you can sustain the routine long enough for the mirror to start talking back.
